I’ve been farming these flat lands of Quzhou County for over forty years, and at sixty-five, I don’t see any reason to change what works. My bones ache more than they used to, and my son works in Shijiazhuang now, so it’s mostly me and my wife managing the fields. That means I stick to the double-cropping system I know by heart: winter wheat followed by summer corn. The government still gives us a grain subsidy, and there’s always a buyer for wheat and corn at the local grain station. I have six mu of good irrigated land. The wheat is already in the ground from last October—it greened up nicely after the overwintering irrigation. Now I need to top-dress it with urea at the jointing stage, irrigate two more times, and spray for aphids and powdery mildew. After harvest in early June, I’ll immediately rotary-till and plant hybrid corn. For the corn, I’ll apply compound fertilizer at sowing, side-dress nitrogen at the big-flare stage, irrigate twice if the summer drought hits, and spray pesticides twice to control corn borer and armyworm. I use improved wheat seeds and hybrid corn seeds because the yield difference is too big to ignore. I’m too old to chase risky specialty crops with unstable markets; I want predictable income and manageable labor.
